hints: Look at what fumes each potassium halide makes with concentrated sulfuric acid, and whether those fumes can oxidise iodide.
Reaction 1 only produces $\text{HCl}$ fumes, which are too weak an oxidising agent to turn colourless $\text{I}^-$ into brown $\text{I}_2$.
For reaction 2, remember what excess ammonia does to a silver chloride precipitate and link both observations to pick the matching row.
walkthrough:
**Analyse Reaction 1 - Acid plus chloride**

Think of concentrated sulfuric acid as both an acid and an oxidiser. With $\text{KCl}$ only the acid behaviour happens.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{KCl} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{KHSO}_4 + \text{HCl}$$

**Test the fumes with iodide**

The $\text{HCl}$ fumes dissolve in the $\text{KI(aq)}$ but $\text{HCl}$ cannot oxidise $\text{I}^-$ to $\text{I}_2$. Only $\text{HBr}$ and $\text{HI}$ made from bromides and iodides are oxidised further to give brown $\text{Br}_2$ or $\text{I}_2$.

So no brown colour appears, the $\text{KI}$ solution stays colourless.

**Analyse Reaction 2 - Silver ions in ammonia**

Normally silver ions and chloride ions give a white precipitate:
$$\text{Ag}^+ + \text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{AgCl(s, white)}$$

**Add the effect of excess ammonia**

Here the $\text{Cl}^-$ is already mixed with excess aqueous ammonia. Any $\text{AgCl}$ that tries to form dissolves as a soluble complex ion.

Complex formation:
$$\text{AgCl} + 2\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow [\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+ + \text{Cl}^-$$
This gives a colourless solution with no white precipitate. Colourless in reaction 1 plus colourless in reaction 2 matches one row.

options.A: Incorrect. Brown solution in reaction 1 would mean $\text{I}_2$ formed. That happens with $\text{KBr}$ or $\text{KI}$ plus concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, not with $\text{KCl}$ because $\text{HCl}$ is not oxidised.
options.B: Incorrect on both counts. Reaction 1 stays colourless as above, and reaction 2 gives no white $\text{AgCl}$ precipitate because excess $\text{NH}_3$ keeps silver in solution as $[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+$. This option confuses chloride with bromide or iodide chemistry.
options.C: Correct. Reaction 1 gives only $\text{HCl}$ fumes which cannot oxidise $\text{I}^-$, so the $\text{KI}$ solution stays colourless. Reaction 2 gives no precipitate because $\text{AgCl}$ dissolves in excess ammonia to form the colourless complex $[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+$. Colourless plus colourless is observed.
options.D: Half right but half wrong. Colourless solution for reaction 1 is correct, but white precipitate for reaction 2 is the normal $\text{AgCl}$ test without ammonia. Students choosing this forget that dissolving $\text{KCl}$ in aqueous ammonia first prevents the precipitate by complex formation.
